finalText:
`async` and `defer` only change behaviour for scripts that the parser has to download. Both let the browser keep parsing the HTML while the file downloads. They differ in when the script runs. A `defer` script waits until the whole document is parsed, runs in document order, and finishes before `DOMContentLoaded`. An `async` script runs as soon as it arrives, in no guaranteed order, and doesn't hold up `DOMContentLoaded`.

**Baseline: a plain `<script src>` with neither attribute.** The HTML spec says such a script "is fetched and evaluated immediately, blocking parsing until these are both complete" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html).

**`async` (classic script with `src`)**
- **Parsing:** The file is "fetched in parallel to parsing and evaluated as soon as it is available (potentially before parsing completes)" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html). Downloading doesn't block parsing, but running the script can. web.dev notes that async scripts "can interrupt DOM building if they finish downloading while the parser is still at work" (https://web.dev/articles/efficiently-load-third-party-javascript).
- **Order:** None is guaranteed. In the spec's algorithm, async scripts go into a *set* of scripts that "will execute as soon as possible", and each one runs on its own once it's ready (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html). MDN puts it as "You get no guarantee that scripts will run in any specific order" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script).
- **`DOMContentLoaded`:** It doesn't wait for async scripts (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event). web.dev says they run "before the window's load event" (https://web.dev/articles/efficiently-load-third-party-javascript). So an async script can run before or after `DOMContentLoaded`, depending on when it finishes downloading.
- **Sources disagree on one point.** MDN's `DOMContentLoaded` page says the event "is fired after the execution of these scripts, but before the execution of scripts with async" (same MDN URL). The spec says an async script can run "potentially before parsing completes", which means before `DOMContentLoaded`. I'd follow the spec: the MDN sentence describes a typical case, not a guarantee. A script loaded with `async` may find the event has already fired, so it should check `document.readyState`, as MDN itself recommends.

**`defer` (classic script with `src`)**
- **Parsing:** The file is "fetched in parallel and evaluated when the page has finished parsing" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html), so it never blocks the parser.
- **Order:** Deferred scripts go into a *list* of scripts that "will execute when the document has finished parsing", and run in that order (spec URL above). MDN: "Scripts with the defer attribute will execute in the order in which they appear in the document" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script).
- **`DOMContentLoaded`:** Deferred scripts run after parsing finishes and before the event fires. They "will prevent the DOMContentLoaded event from firing until the script has loaded and finished evaluating" (same MDN URL). `document.readyState` is already `"interactive"` while they run (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event).
- **A wording problem in MDN:** the summary list on MDN's `<script>` page says defer scripts "will only execute once everything has finished loading". That conflicts with MDN's own attribute description and with the spec. It really means "once parsing has finished", not after the `load` event.

**Using both attributes together:** `async` wins (MDN). The spec says you can include `defer` as well so that very old browsers that only understand `defer` fall back to it instead of blocking (spec URL).

**Inline classic scripts (no `src`)**
- The spec's table doesn't allow `async` or `defer` on inline classic scripts. MDN warns that adding them "would have no effect".
- Inline scripts without `type="module"` "are fetched and executed immediately before the browser continues to parse the page" (MDN `<script>` page). One exception: if a stylesheet that blocks scripts is still loading, the inline script waits for it, and the parser waits too.

**`type="module"` scripts**
- **Default behaviour is like `defer`:** Without `async`, a module script and its dependencies are fetched in parallel to parsing and run once parsing has finished. "The defer attribute has no effect on module scripts" (spec URL).
- **Ordering:** Module scripts join the same in-order, after-parsing list as deferred classic scripts, and `DOMContentLoaded` waits for them (MDN `DOMContentLoaded` page).
- **With `async`:** The module and all its dependencies are fetched in parallel and the module runs "as soon as it is available".
- **Inline modules work differently from inline classic scripts.** `async` is allowed on them. Without it, an inline module is still put off until parsing finishes, and it never runs synchronously. The spec says this holds "even if the inline module script has no dependencies".

**Scripts added by JavaScript:** By default, scripts inserted dynamically are treated as async ("force async"). If you set `async = false`, they go into a list of scripts that "execute in order as soon as possible" (spec URL).
